name: Routing Across Automated Market Makers
title: Routing Across Automated Market Makers
answer: Routing across automated market makers covers the process of finding and executing a trade through one or more on-chain liquidity pools to achieve the best available outcome. It includes splitting a single order across multiple pools, sequencing multi-hop trades through intermediate tokens, and comparing direct routes against aggregated paths. The scope also extends to gas cost awareness, slippage estimation, and protection against adverse execution such as sandwich attacks. Practitioners in this area work with decentralised exchanges, liquidity pools, and solver or aggregator systems that operate across blockchains.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Routing across automated market makers covers the process of finding and executing a trade through one or more on-chain liquidity pools to achieve the best available outcome. It includes splitting a single order across multiple pools, sequencing multi-hop trades through intermediate tokens, and comparing direct routes against aggregated paths. The scope also extends to gas cost awareness, slippage estimation, and protection against adverse execution such as sandwich attacks. Practitioners in this area work with decentralised exchanges, liquidity pools, and solver or aggregator systems that operate across blockchains.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Routing systems run on a combination of off-chain computation and on-chain settlement. Off-chain components include indexers that track pool states, RPC nodes that read blockchain data, mempool monitors that observe pending transactions, and gas price oracles. On-chain components are the automated market maker smart contracts themselves, along with router contracts that execute multi-step swaps atomically. Some designs use intent-based infrastructure where users submit desired outcomes and a network of solvers competes to fill them, while others rely on centralised quote APIs that aggregate liquidity data before sending a transaction.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by modelling each pool as a node or edge in a graph and searching for paths that minimise total cost, including price impact, pool fees, and gas. Constant product and other pricing curves are used to compute how much a given trade size moves the price in each pool. Optimisation techniques include shortest path search, dynamic programming, and linear or convex optimisation for splitting orders across parallel routes. Some systems use machine learning to predict short-term gas prices, pool liquidity changes, or the likelihood of a transaction being front-run, and then adjust routing decisions accordingly.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risks in routing centre on execution quality, transparency, and exposure to miner or validator extractable value. Users face risks from stale quotes, failed transactions, sandwich attacks, and smart contract vulnerabilities in router or pool code. Data provenance matters because routing decisions depend on pool states and mempool observations that can be manipulated or delayed by RPC providers and relayers. Slippage tolerances and transaction deadlines give users some control, but private order flow and exclusive liquidity arrangements can shift who captures value. Regulatory treatment of routing services remains unsettled in many jurisdictions, so operators track compliance obligations without relying on this text as legal guidance.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Routing is moving toward intent-based execution, where users express a desired outcome and specialised solvers compete to fill it across multiple venues, including off-chain liquidity. Cross-chain routing is becoming more common as bridges and messaging protocols allow a single trade to move value across different blockchains. Privacy-preserving order flow and encrypted mempools are being explored to reduce front-running and improve execution for large orders. Machine learning is likely to play a larger role in real-time route selection, gas forecasting, and risk scoring, while wallet and aggregator interfaces continue to absorb routing complexity so that end users see only a final price and confirmation.
